Subject: Enron Board Elects New Corporate Secretary
From: Ken Lay- Chairman of the Board@ENRON <IMCEANOTES-Ken+20Lay-+20Chairman+20of+20the+20Board+40ENRON@ENRON.com>
To: All Enron Worldwide@ENRON <IMCEANOTES-All+20Enron+20Worldwide+40ENRON@ENRON.com>

I am pleased to announce that the Enron Board has selected Paula Rieker to serve as corporate secretary, effective immediately.  She succeeds Rebecca Carter, who has held that position since 1999.  Paula will report jointly to me and Jim Derrick, executive vice president and general counsel.

Paula joined Enron in 1990 and has worked in several areas, including assistant treasurer for Enron Corp., vice president and chief financial officer of Enron Global Power & Pipelines, and vice president of Financial Initiatives in Accounting.  Most recently, she has served as managing director of Investor Relations, a position she has held for the past four years.  Paula will retain a dual role with IR through mid-October.  Paula earned a bachelor's degree in finance from Texas A&M University, and she is a Certified Public Accountant.

Rebecca has been with the company for 11 years and has held a range of positions.  I would like to thank Rebecca for her many years of service to Enron.  Although I am sorry she has chosen to leave, I am grateful that she will remain through the end of January to help ensure a smooth transition of her duties.

Please join me in congratulating Paula on her new responsibilities and wishing Rebecca success in her future endeavors.

Subject: Ethylene margin collar simulation model

I have established the simulation model, with the margin represented by a mean-reverting process.

I divided the data into two categories: margin >0.04 and margin <0.04.
I then estimated the mean-reversion speed separately for each of these data sets.
The resulting mean-reversion speed was higher than the estimate based on the entire data
set.

The greater MR speed reduces the probability on the high-payout side.
Because the MR speed depends on where the data is divided, Bob will run
several senarios.

I included the overall settlement cap and floor in the montly premium
calculation, so the
value in E18 on the summary page is the final answer for pricing the deal.
I also computed the undiscounted payout distribution and the total collar
worth.

Relaxing the overall cap and floor will provide a direct comparison with the spread option
approach that Bob and Lee established.  

It looks like we have a reasonable model.

Subject: Option pricing discrepancy for J.C. Penny Transaction

Amitava and Seksan have determined the cause of the difference between the 
option prices produced by the credit-reserve model and those from the stand-alone 
spreadsheet model used for deal pricing. The difference results from 
variations in the models’ input variables rather than from any algorithmic 
differences.

The options being valued comprise a strip of options on monthly instruments. The 
credit reserve simulation program determines the time to expiration by 
assuming that the option expires on the first day of the underlying contract’s 
contract month, which is a very reasonable assumption.

The stand-alone option pricing spreadsheet permits the option expiration date 
to be specified separately from the underlying contract’s contract month. In 
the JC Penney transaction, the monthly options were assumed to expire in the 
middle of the contract month, although the underlying monthly contracts actually 
expire before the beginning of their respective contract months. The 
stand-alone spreadsheet model permits these specifications, and the user must 
verify that the expiration dates entered are legal. At present, Seksan is 
checking whether the option contracts involved are indeed monthly options rather 
than a strip of daily options; if they are daily options, we would need 
estimates of intramonth volatilities for both the spreadsheet model and the 
credit reserve model.
